title: Topic picker: a broad list
subtitle: Tick the topics you want (Hayk, 2026-11-28: "a lot more various topics, I don't want such narrow concentration"). Hooks are from memory, not yet fact-checked: each picked topic gets a full check before any script. Already picked (11): small places at both extremes, London's V-1 bombs, Monty Hall, the anchoring wheel, leap years, why the sky is blue, birthday paradox, the chocolate hoax, Hanoi's rats, seasons and the tilt, tickling yourself. You can still select any text and press C to comment.

items.title: Why we get goosebumps
items.note: A leftover reflex from furry ancestors: hair standing up to look bigger or keep warm.

items.title: Why fingers wrinkle in water
items.note: Not soaking: nerves shrink the blood vessels, maybe for grip on wet things (still debated).

items.title: Why nobody remembers being a baby
items.note: Childhood amnesia: memories form, but the brain's indexing is not ready to keep them.

items.title: Why time speeds up as we age
items.note: Fewer new memories make years feel shorter; a year is also a smaller share of your life.

items.title: How much of your body is bacteria?
items.note: The old '10 bacteria per human cell' was wrong: closer to 1 to 1.

items.title: Why the appendix is not useless
items.note: It seems to store good gut bacteria for after an illness.

items.title: Why about 1 in 10 people is left-handed
items.note: The ratio is old and stable across cultures; what genes and the womb do.

items.title: Why zebras have stripes
items.note: Experiments with horses in striped coats: biting flies fail to land.

items.title: Why flamingos are pink
items.note: Their food: chicks are grey; no shrimp, no pink.

items.title: Does a goldfish remember only 3 seconds?
items.note: A myth: they remember for months and can be trained.

items.title: How birds find their way south
items.note: A magnetic sense in the eye, the stars, smell: still being worked out.

items.title: Octopus: three hearts and blue blood
items.note: And most of its neurons are in its arms.

items.title: Why leaves turn yellow and red
items.note: The yellow was there all summer under the green; the red is made fresh.

items.title: Tardigrades: the animal that survived space
items.note: Dried out, they survive vacuum, radiation and freezing.

items.title: Why cats purr
items.note: We know how, roughly, but not fully why: it is not only happiness.

items.title: Why the night sky is dark
items.note: Olbers' paradox: an endless, eternal universe would glow everywhere; the dark sky says it had a beginning.

items.title: If the Sun vanished, we would notice 8 minutes later
items.note: Light and gravity travel at the same speed.

items.title: Why Pluto stopped being a planet
items.note: The 2006 vote and the three-rule definition.

items.title: Why Venus is hotter than Mercury
items.note: Farther from the Sun but wrapped in CO2: a greenhouse gone wild.

items.title: How we know the Earth is 4.5 billion years old
items.note: Radioactive clocks in rocks and meteorites.

items.title: Why the sea has two tides a day
items.note: The Moon pulls the near side and leaves the far side behind.

items.title: Why the ocean is blue
items.note: Not only the sky's reflection: water itself absorbs red light.

items.title: Why Armenia has earthquakes
items.note: The Arabian plate pushing north; how the land moves each year (careful framing around 1988).

items.title: Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature
items.note: Your hand senses heat flow, not temperature.

items.title: Do mirrors flip left and right?
items.note: No: they flip front and back. Why it looks like left-right.

items.title: Why a coffee stain dries as a ring
items.note: The edge holds and liquid flows outwards carrying the grains (a 1997 Nature paper).

items.title: How a microwave heats food
items.note: Water molecules spinning; why the middle stays cold; the myths.

items.title: Why popcorn pops
items.note: Water inside each kernel becomes steam until the shell bursts at about 180 °C.

items.title: Why glass is transparent
items.note: Visible light has the wrong energy for glass's electrons to absorb.

items.title: Why ice is slippery
items.note: Still debated: the old pressure explanation is wrong.

items.title: How GPS knows where you are, and needs Einstein
items.note: Satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day; uncorrected, maps would drift about 10 km a day.

items.title: The internet lives on the sea floor
items.note: Almost all traffic between continents runs through undersea cables.

items.title: Why a torn QR code still works
items.note: Error correction: up to about 30% can be missing.

items.title: Why phone batteries die in the cold
items.note: Chemistry slows down; the charge is still there.

items.title: Why 'Save' is a floppy disk
items.note: Icons outliving their objects (skeuomorphs): the phone handset, the envelope.

items.title: How noise-cancelling headphones work
items.note: They play the noise back upside down.

items.title: Why airliners fly at 10-12 km
items.note: Thin air means less drag; too high and the engines starve.

items.title: How a touchscreen feels your finger
items.note: Your body is part of an electric circuit; why gloves don't work.

items.title: The Great Emu War, 1932
items.note: The Australian army went after emus with machine guns, and the emus won.

items.title: The dancing plague of 1518
items.note: People in Strasbourg danced for days; what historians think happened.

items.title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
items.note: Time perspective: deep time drawn to scale.

items.title: The Library of Alexandria did not burn in one fire
items.note: It faded over centuries; the single fire is a myth.

items.title: Napoleon was not short
items.note: French vs English inches, and British cartoons.

items.title: Vikings never wore horned helmets
items.note: The horns come from 19th-century opera costumes.

items.title: 1816, the year without a summer
items.note: A volcano in Indonesia, famine in Europe, and Frankenstein.

items.title: The shortest war: about 40 minutes
items.note: Britain vs Zanzibar, 1896.

items.title: Why 'mama' sounds alike in many languages
items.note: The easiest sounds a baby makes, and parents claiming them.

items.title: How 'OK' took over the world
items.note: An 1830s newspaper joke ('oll korrect') that survived.

items.title: How many words do you know?
items.note: Adults know tens of thousands; how researchers count them.

items.title: Why some scripts run right to left
items.note: Carving, ink, and habit: the history behind the direction.

items.title: Words Armenian lent to the world, and borrowed
items.note: From Persian, Greek, Russian; and the few going the other way.

items.title: Why every language has filler words
items.note: 'Um' and 'eh' are signals, not mistakes (research on fillers).

items.title: Why paper money is worth anything
items.note: Trust; the giant stone money of Yap, where stones never moved.

items.title: Why prices end in 990
items.note: The left-digit effect: 9,990 dram feels like 9 thousand.

items.title: Why the milk is at the back of the shop
items.note: You walk past everything else (and the cold-room story).

items.title: Inflation: a wheelbarrow of money for bread
items.note: Germany 1923 and Zimbabwe; how prices run away.

items.title: The tragedy of the commons
items.note: Why shared things get used up, and how communities avoid it (Ostrom).

items.title: Why the dram is called the dram
items.note: From the Greek drachma; Armenia's 1993 currency.

items.title: Why chilli burns
items.note: It switches on your heat sensor (a 2021 Nobel prize).

items.title: Why bread goes stale
items.note: Not drying out: the starch recrystallises; a toaster reverses it.

items.title: Why honey never goes bad
items.note: Too little water and too acidic for microbes.

items.title: Is the 5-second rule real?
items.note: Bacteria jump on in under a second; wet food picks up more.

items.title: Why coriander tastes of soap to some people
items.note: A smell gene; how common it is.

items.title: Lavash and the tonir
items.note: How the oven works and why it is on UNESCO's list (local).

items.title: The Mona Lisa became famous because it was stolen
items.note: 1911: the empty wall drew crowds.

items.title: Ultramarine: a blue dearer than gold
items.note: Ground lapis from Afghanistan, saved for the Virgin's robe.

items.title: Why songs get stuck in your head
items.note: Earworms: what research says and how to stop one.

items.title: Why music gives you chills
items.note: Dopamine at the moment the brain's prediction resolves.

items.title: Why there are 12 notes in an octave
items.note: Frequency ratios, Pythagoras, and the compromise of equal temperament.

items.title: Komitas and the songs he saved
items.note: Recording village songs before they were lost (local).

items.title: How zero became a number
items.note: From an empty place in Babylonian numbers to India's 'shunya'.

items.title: How many times can you fold paper?
items.note: The '7 times' myth; a student folded it 12 times in 2002.

items.title: Some infinities are bigger than others
items.note: Hilbert's hotel, and Cantor's diagonal.

items.title: Six degrees of separation
items.note: Milgram's letters and Facebook's 3.5.

items.title: How many piano tuners are in Yerevan?
items.note: Fermi estimates: getting close with rough guesses.

items.title: The wheat and the chessboard
items.note: Doubling 64 times: more grain than the world has ever grown.

items.title: Benford's law: why 1 is the commonest first digit
items.note: About 30% of real numbers start with 1; it catches fraud.

items.title: The ox and the crowd
items.note: 1906: the average of 787 guesses hit an ox's weight almost exactly (wisdom of crowds).

items.title: The Stanford prison experiment, re-checked
items.note: Guards were coached; what it really shows.

items.title: Milgram's shocks: what actually happened
items.note: Many participants doubted it was real; the variations matter.

items.title: Why we procrastinate
items.note: Mood repair, not laziness; what helps.

items.title: Why we like what we have heard before
items.note: The mere-exposure effect: familiar feels good.

items.title: Why confident people get believed
items.note: Confidence as a signal, and when it misleads.

items.title: Why antibiotics do nothing against a cold
items.note: Viruses vs bacteria, and resistance.

items.title: The milkmaid and the first vaccine
items.note: Jenner, cowpox, and where the word 'vaccine' comes from (vacca, cow).

items.title: Penicillin: a mouldy dish from a holiday
items.note: Fleming 1928, and the 12 years before it could be made.

items.title: Semmelweis: wash your hands
items.note: He cut deaths with handwashing and was mocked.

items.title: Do we use only 10% of the brain?
items.note: No: scans show all of it working; where the myth came from.

items.title: What happens after a night without sleep
items.note: Reaction time like being drunk; what sleep does.

items.title: Why golf balls have dimples
items.note: Dimples make it fly about twice as far.

items.title: How a ball curves (Magnus effect)
items.note: Roberto Carlos's 1997 free kick.

items.title: Penalty kicks: the goalkeeper should stay put
items.note: Keepers dive because doing nothing looks worse (2007 study).

items.title: Home advantage and empty stadiums
items.note: COVID games without crowds as a natural experiment.

items.title: Why a marathon is 42.195 km
items.note: The 1908 London route and the royal box.

items.title: Why chess players' brains get tired
items.note: Hours of thinking burn real energy; what studies measured.

items.title: Why African borders are straight lines
items.note: Drawn on maps in Berlin, 1884.

items.title: Why the Dead Sea is dead
items.note: Ten times saltier than the ocean, and shrinking.

items.title: Why the capital is often not the biggest city
items.note: Canberra, Ottawa, Washington: compromise capitals.

items.title: Lake Sevan lost 20 metres
items.note: The Soviet irrigation plan and the tunnel that saved it (local).

items.title: Why Russia has 11 time zones but China one
items.note: Clocks as politics.

items.title: Why the Equator is not the hottest place
items.note: Clouds and rain; the hottest places are deserts near 25-30°.

items.title: Why Armenian apricot wood makes the duduk
items.note: Density and resonance of the wood.

items.title: The oldest leather shoe: Areni-1
items.note: A 5,500-year-old shoe from a cave in Vayots Dzor; how it survived.

items.title: The oldest winery: Areni-1
items.note: 6,100-year-old wine-making equipment from the same cave.

items.title: Why Ararat is in Turkey but on our coat of arms
items.note: Borders of 1921 and a mountain as a symbol (careful framing).

items.title: Carahunge (Zorats Karer): an ancient observatory?
items.note: Holes in the stones and what archaeologists actually conclude.

items.title: Why Armenian has 'ու' as one letter made of two
items.note: Mashtots borrowing the Greek habit (could join the Mashtots video).
